where $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}$ is generated by $Z=-J_{2}-{r\over 2}$ [158] (see also Appendix B), our setup generalizes straightforwardly to more general ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ SCFTs in $d=4$ with type IIB string theory duals on ${\rm AdS}_{5}\times{\rm SE}_{5}$ where ${\rm SE}_{5}$ denotes a general Sasaki-Einstein manifold that replaces the $S^{5}$ in the ${\mathcal{N}}=4$ case. In particular, the supersymmetric black hole solutions reviewed in Section 2.1 only rely on the universal 5d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ supergravity sector and thus remains valid for these more general SCFTs. A detailed analysis of the matching of the bare superconformal index of these more general theories to gravity can be found in [159, 160, 37]. The relevant surface defects that refines the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ (universal) superconformal index here preserve the ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ superconformal symmetry together with the $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}$ commutant in (4.4). On the gravity side, these surface defect probes are described by D3-branes wrapping an orbit of the Reeb vector field on ${\rm SE}_{5}$ and extend in ${\rm AdS}_{5}$ (see [161] for an example). On the field theory side, they are generalizations of the Gukov-Witten surface defects, whose explicit descriptions are more complicated in general. Nonetheless, we expect our bulk analysis to go through, leading to the following conjecture for the surface defect expectation value in general 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ SCFTs, in the large $N$ limit,

$$ \displaystyle\log\,\langle{\mathcal{D}}\rangle=\pi i{(\sigma+\tau-1)^{2}\over 27\sigma}b_{\rm 2d}({\mathcal{D}})\,, $$

where $b_{\rm 2d}({\mathcal{D}})$ is the defect central charge (and $b_{\rm 2d}\ll N^{2}$ ) for the ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ supersymmetric surface defect ${\mathcal{D}}$ . Similarly we expect the same to follow from the generalized Cardy limit for the defect index as described in Section 4.5. It would be interesting to derive this directly from the field theory.

Finally, our setup generalizes to defect indices in other spacetime dimensions, where the probes are provided by other types of branes. For example, the 6d ${\mathcal{N}}=(2,0)$ SCFTs of the $A_{N-1}$ type contain two types of half-BPS surface defects that correspond either to M2-branes in the bulk M-theory on ${\rm AdS}_{7}\times S^{4}$ that sit at a point on the $S^{4}$ [162, 163, 164] or to M5-branes wrapping $S^{3}\subset S^{4}$ [163, 165, 166, 164]. Similarly, in the 3d ${\mathcal{N}}=8$ ABJM SCFTs which have M-theory duals on ${\rm AdS}_{4}\times S^{7}$ , a class of half-BPS surface defects are described by M5 branes wrapping $S^{3}\subset S^{7}$ [163, 167, 164]. It would be interesting to investigate such brane probes in relation to the confinement/deconfinement phase transitions in these spacetime dimensions and the possibility of probing black holes in the dual AdS spaces.

## Appendix A Calibrated D3-brane in the black hole geometry

The AdS5 black holes we are considering (viewed as 10d solutions of type IIB supergravity) preserve ${1\over 16}$ -th of the supersymmetry. This is also the minimum required supersymmetry for a BPS state in the dual $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory. In the presence of a probe D3-brane, it is a non-trivial requirement that the full bulk + defect system preserve this required amount of supersymmetry due to the presence of the brane. At the level of the probe worldvolume action (2.20), we have only given the bosonic terms, but this should always be supplemented by terms involving worldvolume fermions determined by supersymmetry. Naively, a purely bosonic embedding into the 10d target space can never be supersymmetric because a supersymmetry variation parametrized by the bulk killing spinor turns on these fermions. Supersymmetry is only possible when the local fermionic kappa symmetry on the worldvolume may be used to gauge away this variation.

Rather than checking that the total action $S_{\textrm{bulk}}+S_{\textrm{brane}}$ in invariant under the combined supergravity and worldvolume supersymmetries, we will instead check the necessary kappa symmetry projection condition [168, 169, 170, 171]. Similar supersymmetric brane configurations were considered in [45], and we closely follow these conventions in what follows. The primary difference is that the branes considered here extend out to the AdS boundary, and it is nontrivial to show that the supersymmetries preserved by this profile and the supersymmetries preseved by the black hole are compatible.3535 35 See [90, 91] for similar studies for D3-branes in empty AdS.

If $\varepsilon$ is a bulk Killing spinor satisfying

$$ \hat{D}_{M}\varepsilon=\left(\partial_{M}+\frac{1}{4}\omega^{AB}_{M}\Gamma_{AB}+\frac{i}{16\cdot 5!}F_{N_{1}N_{2}\dots N_{5}}\Gamma^{N_{1}N_{2}\dots N_{5}}\Gamma_{M}\right)\varepsilon=0\,, $$

then the kappa symmetry projection condition is

$$ \Theta\varepsilon=\mp i\varepsilon\,, $$

where

$$ \Theta=\frac{1}{4!}\frac{\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}}{\sqrt{-h}}\frac{\partial X^{M}}{\partial\sigma^{\alpha}}\frac{\partial X^{N}}{\partial\sigma^{\beta}}\frac{\partial X^{P}}{\partial\sigma^{\gamma}}\frac{\partial X^{Q}}{\partial\sigma^{\delta}}\Gamma_{MNPQ}\,, $$

where $\sigma^{\alpha}$ are the worldvolume coordinates of the brane and $\sqrt{-h}$ is the volume of the pullback metric in Lorentzian signature. We have chosen the Lorentzian problem to avoid the complications of supersymmetry in Euclidean signature. We assume that a kappa symmetric brane configuration may safely be continued to Euclidean where the metric will in general be complex and non-extremal. We will see that the existence of supersymmetric (but finite temperature) black hole solutions implies the existence of kappa symmetric brane configurations on the non-extremal background.

In the main text, we chose the coordinates in (2.3) to evaluate the action of the D3-brane. However, as in [45], for the purpose of studying supersymmetric embedding, it is convenient to introduce orthotoric coordinates [121] $(t,\xi,\eta,\Phi,\Psi)$ on the AdS black hole part of the spacetime, as well as new coordinates $(\rho_{s},\theta_{s},\varphi_{s},\zeta_{s},\psi_{s})$ on the $S^{5}$ . These coordinates are related to the original ones (2.3) via:

$$ \displaystyle r^{2} \displaystyle=r_{*}^{2}+(a+b)\,\widetilde{m}+\frac{(a+b)^{2}}{2}\,\widetilde{m}+\frac{a^{2}-b^{2}}{2}\,\widetilde{m}\,\xi\,,\quad\quad\quad\theta=\frac{1}{2}\arccos(\eta)\,, \displaystyle\phi \displaystyle=t+\frac{4(1-a^{2})}{(a^{2}-b^{2})\widetilde{m}}\,(\Psi-\Phi)\,,\quad\quad\quad\psi=t-\frac{4(1-b^{2})}{(a^{2}-b^{2})\widetilde{m}}\,(\Phi+\Psi)\,, \displaystyle\mu_{1} \displaystyle=\sin\rho_{s}\cos\frac{\theta_{s}}{2}\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad\phi_{1}=\frac{1}{6}(2\psi_{s}+\zeta_{s}-3\varphi_{s})\,, \displaystyle\mu_{2} \displaystyle=\sin\rho_{s}\sin\frac{\theta_{s}}{2}\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad\phi_{2}=\frac{1}{6}(2\psi_{s}+\zeta_{s}+3\varphi_{s})\,, \displaystyle\mu_{3} \displaystyle=\cos\rho_{s}\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\,\,\,\phi_{3}=\frac{1}{3}(\psi_{s}-\zeta_{s})\,, $$

where the new angular variables take the ranges $0\leq\rho_{s}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}$ , $0\leq\theta_{s}\leq\pi$ , $0\leq\varphi_{s}<2\pi$ , $0\leq\zeta_{s}<4\pi$ , and $0\leq\psi_{s}<6\pi$ . We also use a new mass parameter

$$ \widetilde{m}=\frac{m}{(a+b)(1+a)(1+b)(1+a+b)}-1\;. $$

In the extremal limit, $\widetilde{m}=0$ and we could consider taking this limit before evaluating the supersymmetry condition of the brane. However, our coordinate system has naive singularities for $\widetilde{m}=0$ so this limit would need to be taken with care. Instead, we will find supersymmetric brane configurations for any value of $\widetilde{m}$ ; this corresponds to the fact that in Euclidean signature the supersymmetric and $T=0$ conditions of the gravity background are decoupled [23]. Additionally note that the equal rotation limit of $a=b$ is also singular in these coordinates. We’ve independently verified the kappa symmetry condition in the metric suitable for the $a=b$ limit, even though we do not focus on this case in our paper.

The advantage of using orthotoric coordinates is that the vielbeins and gauge potential are mostly diagonal and may be written in terms of a few simple functions of ${\mathcal{G}},{\mathcal{F}},f,\omega$ of $\xi,\eta$ :

$$ \displaystyle e^{0}=f(dt-\omega)\,,\quad e^{1}=\,\sqrt{\frac{\eta-\xi}{{\mathcal{F}}(\xi)\,f}}\,d\xi\,,\quad e^{2}=\,\sqrt{\frac{{\mathcal{F}}(\xi)}{(\eta-\xi)\,f}}\,\bigl(d\Phi+\eta\,d\Psi\bigr)\,,\quad e^{3}=-\,\sqrt{\frac{\eta-\xi}{{\mathcal{G}}(\eta)\,f}}\,d\eta\,, $$

$$ \displaystyle e^{4}=\,\sqrt{\frac{{\mathcal{G}}(\eta)}{(\eta-\xi)\,f}}\,\bigl(d\Phi+\xi\,d\Psi\bigr)\,,\quad\quad e^{5}=d\rho_{s}\,,\quad\quad e^{6}=\frac{1}{4}\sin(2\rho_{s})\,\bigl(d\zeta_{s}-\cos(\theta_{s})\,d\varphi_{s}\bigr)\,, $$

$$ \displaystyle e^{7}=\frac{1}{2}\sin(\rho_{s})\,d\theta_{s}\,,\quad e^{8}=\frac{1}{2}\sin(\rho_{s})\,\sin(\theta_{s})\,d\varphi_{s}\,,\quad e^{9}=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(d\psi_{s}+\mathcal{A}+2A_{(1)}\bigr)\,, \displaystyle\mathcal{A}=3\tan(\rho_{s})\,e^{6}-d\zeta_{s}\,, \displaystyle A_{(1)}=-\frac{6(1+a)(1+b)(1+\widetilde{m})f}{(a^{2}-b^{2})(a-b)\widetilde{m}^{2}(\eta-\xi)}\,\biggl[\left(a+b-(a-b)\eta\right)d\Phi+\left((a+b)\eta-(a-b)\right)d\Psi\biggr]\, \displaystyle+\frac{3(1-f)}{2}dt-\alpha\,dt\,, $$

where we have used the functions,

$$ \displaystyle{\displaystyle\mathcal{G}}(\eta)=-\frac{4\,(1-\eta^{2})}{(a^{2}-b^{2})\,\widetilde{m}}\,\Bigl[(1-a^{2})(1+\eta)+(1-b^{2})(1-\eta)\Bigr]\,, \displaystyle{\displaystyle\mathcal{F}}(\xi)=-{\mathcal{G}}(\xi)-4\,\frac{1+\widetilde{m}}{\widetilde{m}}\left(\frac{2+a+b+(a-b)\xi}{a-b}\right)^{3}\,, \displaystyle f=-\frac{\widetilde{m}\,(a-b)\,(\eta-\xi)}{(2+a+b)(1+\widetilde{m})+(a-b)(\eta+\widetilde{m}\xi)}\,, \displaystyle\omega=\frac{{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime\prime}\,{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime\prime\prime}}{288}\Bigl[(\eta+\xi)\,d\Phi+\eta\,\xi\,d\Psi\Bigr]+\frac{2}{\widetilde{m}}\,d\Psi \displaystyle-\frac{{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime\prime}+{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime\prime\prime}}{48\,(\eta-\xi)^{2}}\left\{\left[{\mathcal{F}}+(\eta-\xi)\left(\frac{{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime}}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{2+a+b}{a-b}+\xi\right)^{2}{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime\prime}\right)\right](d\Phi+\eta\,d\Psi)+{\mathcal{G}}\,(d\Phi+\xi\,d\Psi)\right\}. $$

In addition to the 10d metric in the new coordinates, the equations of motion demand a specific choice of the self-dual RR 5-form $F_{(5)}$ which we have not yet written. This form includes the volume form of AdS plus its dual, but also additional terms due to the rotation of the black hole on the $S^{5}$ . Up to gauge transformation, one may then find a gauge field $C_{(4)}$ such that $F_{(5)}=dC_{(4)}$ . The one form $\mathcal{A}$ enters the expression for $C_{(4)}$ . The natural choice giving a valid solution for $F_{(5)}$ in our coordinates (A.8) is singular on the brane worldvolume where $\rho_{s}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\theta_{s}=0$ ; the circles corresponding to $\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=0$ are shrinking, so similar to [45] we perform a gauge transformation to remove the $\phi_{2}$ and $\phi_{3}$ components from $\mathcal{A}$ :

$$ \mathcal{A}\rightarrow\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\mathcal{A}+d\psi_{s}\,. $$

When evaluated on the worldvolume, $\rho_{s}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ , $\theta_{s}=0$ , one obtains $\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=3d\phi_{1}$ , leading to the quantization condition $\int\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=6\pi$ and a nonsingular choice of $C_{(4)}$ :

$$ C_{(4)}=-4\beta_{(4)}+\frac{1}{9}\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\wedge\left[\ast_{5}F_{(2)}+\left(\frac{1}{2}d\tilde{\mathcal{A}}-F_{(2)}\right)\wedge e^{9}\right]\,, $$

where $\beta_{(4)}$ is any 4-form such that $d\beta_{(4)}=\epsilon_{(5)}$ is the volume form of the 5d asymptotically AdS metric and $F_{(2)}=dA_{(1)}$ is the 5d gauge field strength. The $F_{(5)}=dC_{(4)}$ derived from the above expression solves the 10d equations of motion, but we do not need its explicit form. This is the expression we utilized in Section 2.2 to evaluate the brane action. Only the $\frac{1}{9}\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\wedge\ast_{5}F_{(2)}$ term in the expression contains components that cover all the brane worldvolume coordinates.

One may explicitly check that this metric is equivalent to the original 10d one used in the main text. Further, the Killing spinor solving (A.1) associated with this solution in these coordinates was reported in [45]. This led to the discovery of a class of wrapped supersymmetric Euclidean D3-branes in AdS ${}_{5}\times S^{5}$ which contribute to the dual superconformal index. The bulk calculation here is almost identical, and we only need to check that (A.3) preserves the kappa symmetry condition for our D3-branes which extend out to the AdS boundary. In the new coordinates, the static gauge embedding of the brane which wraps the $(\sigma^{0},\sigma^{1},\sigma^{2},\sigma^{3})=(t,r,\phi,\phi_{1})$ coordinates is given by

$$ \displaystyle t \displaystyle=\sigma^{0}\,,\quad\xi=\frac{2(a+b+ab)+(a^{2}+b^{2})\widetilde{m}+2(a+b+ab)\widetilde{m}-2(\sigma^{1})^{2}}{(a^{2}-b^{2})\widetilde{m}}\,,\quad\eta=-1\,, \displaystyle\Phi \displaystyle=-\frac{(a^{2}-b^{2})\widetilde{m}}{8(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})}\left((1-a^{2})\psi_{0}+(-2+a^{2}+b^{2})\sigma^{0}+(1-b^{2})\sigma^{2}\right)\,, \displaystyle\Psi \displaystyle=-\frac{(a^{2}-b^{2})\widetilde{m}}{8(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})}\left((a^{2}-b^{2})\sigma^{0}+(1-a^{2})\psi_{0}-(1-b^{2})\sigma^{2}\right)\,, \displaystyle\rho_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{2}\,,\quad\theta_{s}=0\,,\quad\varphi_{s}=\textrm{const}-\sigma^{3}\,,\quad\zeta_{s}=\textrm{const}+\sigma^{3}\,,\quad\psi_{s}=\textrm{const}+\sigma^{3}\,. $$

Here, $\psi_{0}$ was a constant angle where we placed the brane in the original coordinates, and the further constants are similar and do not affect the analysis.

Using the above vielbeins evaluated on this embedding, some computation shows the determinant of the induced metric, $\sqrt{-\textrm{det}(g_{D3})}=\sqrt{-\textrm{det}(\partial_{\alpha}X_{M}\partial_{\beta}X^{M})}$ , is

$$ \sqrt{-\textrm{det}(g_{D3})}=\frac{r}{1-a^{2}}\,. $$

We’ve also done the sanity check that we get the same answer using the coordinate system in (2.3). Further, the combination of pullbacks in (A.3) is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{4!}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\partial_{\alpha}X^{M}\partial_{\beta}X^{N}\partial_{\gamma}X^{P}\partial_{\delta}X^{Q}\Gamma_{MNPQ}=\left(\frac{r}{1-a^{2}}\right)\Gamma_{0129}\,, $$

where $\Gamma_{0129}$ is a particular rank-four Gamma matrix in the frame basis. This allows us to conclude

$$ \Theta=\pm\Gamma_{0129}\,. $$

The reason why a $\pm$ ambiguity appears is because there are square roots found in obtaining the determinant and pullbacks. The sign also relies on the ordering of the worldvolume coordinates. To fully resolve this one would need to more carefully define the orientation of the brane as opposed to an anti-brane. Of course, we know from [95] that it is D3-brane that is supersymmetric on the background instead of anti D3-brane. Up to these choices which affect the overall sign, we see that there exists a projection matrix with this simple form. As discussed in Appendix. C of [45], there exists Killing spinor $\varepsilon$ on the black hole background satisfying

$$ \Gamma_{0129}\,\varepsilon=i\varepsilon, $$

therefore the kappa symmetry projection condition (A.2) holds given the lower sign in (A.18).

Further note that we did not have to make any assumptions about the extremality. Note that no divergences appear in the extremal limit $T=0$ and thus $\widetilde{m}=0$ in the background. We did impose the supersymmetric condition (2.13) on the charge $q$ , which enters implicitly through the definition of the gauge potential $A$ .

## Appendix B Superconformal algebra

In this paper, we consider the insertion of a half-BPS GW surface operator in 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ ${\rm SU}(N)$ SYM, breaking the 4d superconformal algebra to a half-BPS subalgebra,

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}\ltimes(\mathfrak{psu}(1,1|2)\times\mathfrak{psu}(1,1|2))\ltimes\mathfrak{u}(1)_{C}\subset\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)\,, $$

which is a central extension of the usual 2d $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ superconformal algebra by $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{C}$ and we have included the $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}$ that acts as an outer-automorphism on the ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ algebra (and in general is not a symmetry of the surface defect3636 36 In the case of the half-BPS Gukov-Witten surface defect [78], only when ${\beta}={\gamma}=0$ in (1.13) does $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}$ become a symmetry of the defect.).

The Cartan generators for the subalgebra on the LHS of (B.1) can be identified with those in 4d as follows,

$$ \displaystyle L_{0}=\frac{E+J_{1}}{2},\quad\bar{L}_{0}=\frac{E-J_{1}}{2},\quad J_{0}=\frac{R_{2}-R_{3}}{2},\quad\bar{J}_{0}=\frac{R_{2}+R_{3}}{2}\,, \displaystyle J_{A}=R_{1}-R_{2},\quad C=-J_{2}-\frac{R_{1}}{2}\,, $$

where $L_{0}$ and $\bar{L}_{0}$ are the left- and the right-moving Hamiltonians on the 2d worldvolume, $J_{0}$ and $\bar{J}_{0}$ are the Cartan generators for the left- and the right-moving $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ R-symmetries, $J_{A}$ generates the outer-automorphism $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}$ and $C$ generates the central extension $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{C}$ .

We denote the Poincaré supercharges of the ${\mathcal{N}}=4$ superconformal algebra by $Q^{\pm,i},\,\bar{Q}_{\pm,i}$ and their hermitian conjugate conformal supercharges by $S_{\pm,i},\bar{S}^{\pm,i}$ respectively [17], where the index $i=1,2,3,4$ labels the fundamental (upper index) and anti-fundamental (lower index) representations of the $\mathfrak{su}(4)_{R}$ R-symmetry. We list the the charges of $Q^{\pm,i}$ and $\bar{S}^{\pm,i}$ under the Cartan generators $R_{1,2,3}$ below,

$$ \displaystyle i=1 \displaystyle:\,R_{1}=1,\,R_{2}=1,\,R_{3}=1\,, \displaystyle i=2 \displaystyle:\,R_{1}=1,\,R_{2}=-1,\,R_{3}=-1\,, \displaystyle i=3 \displaystyle:\,R_{1}=-1,\,R_{2}=1,\,R_{3}=-1\,, \displaystyle i=4 \displaystyle:\,R_{1}=-1,\,R_{2}=-1,\,R_{3}=1\,, $$

and the charges of $\bar{Q}_{\pm,i}$ and $S_{\pm,i}$ come from flipping the sign of every entry above. The bars on the supercharges keep track of their chiralities and the $\pm$ are the corresponding spinor indices (charge under $\frac{J_{1}+J_{2}}{2}$ for the chiral spinor and $\frac{J_{1}-J_{2}}{2}$ for the anti-chiral spinor).

We denote the left- and the right-moving Poincaré supercharges of the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ algebra by $G^{\pm a}$ and $\bar{G}^{\pm\dot{a}}$ respectively, where $a,\dot{a}=1,2$ are the doublet indices for the left- and the right-moving $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ R-symmetries and $\pm$ keeps track of the charges under $R_{1}$ (which together with (B.2) determines the corresponding charges under the outer-automorphism $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}$ ). The explicit identification between the fermionic generators of the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ algebra and those in the 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=4$ algebra is recorded in Table 2, along with their anticommutation relations.

| 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ | 2d $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ |
|---|---|
| $\{Q^{-,1},S_{-,1}\}=(E-J_{1})-\frac{R_{2}+R_{3}}{2}-(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{\bar{G}^{+,1},(\bar{G}^{+,1})^{\dagger}\}=2\bar{L}_{0}-\bar{J}_{0}+C$ |
| $\{Q^{-,2},S_{-,2}\}=(E-J_{1})-\frac{-R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}-(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{\bar{G}^{+,2},(\bar{G}^{+,2})^{\dagger}\}=2\bar{L}_{0}+\bar{J}_{0}+C$ |
| $\{\bar{Q}_{-,1},\bar{S}^{-,1}\}=(E-J_{1})+\frac{R_{2}+R_{3}}{2}+(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{\bar{G}^{-,2},(\bar{G}^{-,2})^{\dagger}\}=2\bar{L}_{0}+\bar{J}_{0}-C$ |
| $\{\bar{Q}_{-,2},\bar{S}^{-,2}\}=(E-J_{1})+\frac{-R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}+(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{\bar{G}^{-,1},(\bar{G}^{-,1})^{\dagger}\}=2\bar{L}_{0}-\bar{J}_{0}-C$ |
| $\{Q^{+,3},S_{+,3}\}=(E+J_{1})+\frac{-R_{2}+R_{3}}{2}+(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{G^{-,1},(G^{-,1})^{\dagger}\}=2L_{0}-J_{0}-C$ |
| $\{Q^{+,4},S_{+,4}\}=(E+J_{1})+\frac{R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}+(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{G^{-,2},(G^{-,2})^{\dagger}\}=2L_{0}+J_{0}-C$ |
| $\{\bar{Q}_{+,3},\bar{S}^{+,3}\}=(E+J_{1})-\frac{-R_{2}+R_{3}}{2}-(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{G^{+,2},(G^{+,2})^{\dagger}\}=2L_{0}+J_{0}+C$ |
| $\{\bar{Q}_{+,4},\bar{S}^{+,4}\}=(E+J_{1})-\frac{R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}-(J_{2}+\frac{R_{1}}{2})$ | $\{G^{+,1},(G^{+,1})^{\dagger}\}=2L_{0}-J_{0}+C$ |

In particular, the ${1\over 16}$ -BPS superconformal index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm SCI}$ (1.2) is defined by the following complex supercharge and its hermitian conjugate

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{Q}}=Q^{-,1}=\bar{G}^{+,1}\,,\quad{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}=S_{-,1}=(\bar{G}^{+,1})^{\dagger}\,, $$

which are obviously contained the 2d superalgebra (B.1). The bosonic quantum numbers of ${\mathcal{Q}}$ are $E={1\over 2},J_{1,2}=-{1\over 2},R_{1,2,3}=1$ (equivalently $L_{0}=J_{0}=0,2\bar{L}_{0}=\bar{J}_{0}=1,C=J_{A}=0$ ).

In this paper, we consider the GW surface defect ${\mathcal{D}}$ with the continuous parameters restricted to ${\beta}={\gamma}=0$ (see Section 1.2 for a review). In this case, the entire subalgebra in (B.1) including the $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{A}$ outer-automorphism is preserved by ${\mathcal{D}}$ . Consequently, ${\mathcal{D}}$ can be inserted in the ${1\over 16}$ -BPS superconformal index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm SCI}$ , giving rise to the defect index ${\mathcal{I}}_{{\mathcal{D}}}$ (1.23) that count states in the defect Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{D}}(S^{3})$ with the same set of fugacities as for the bare index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm SCI}$ .

Our consideration above generalizes straightforwardly to general superconformal surface defects in general 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ SCFTs (see [100] for a review on superconformal surface defects). Under the most general setup, they are half-BPS surface defects that preserve a 2d $\mathcal{N}=(0,2)$ half-BPS subalgebra in the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal algebra,

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})\times\mathfrak{su}(1,1|1)\times\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}\subset\mathfrak{su}(2,2|1)\,, $$

where $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}$ is the commutant of the 2d superconformal subalgebra. We denote the supercharges for the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal algebra by $({\bm{Q}}^{\pm},{\bm{S}}_{\pm},\bar{\bm{Q}}_{\pm},\bar{\bm{S}}^{\pm})$ . The GW surface operators in the ${\mathcal{N}}=4$ SYM theory are special cases where we identify the 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal algebra as the subalgebra $\mathfrak{su}(2,2|1)\subset\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ generated by

$$ \displaystyle({\bm{Q}}^{\pm},{\bm{S}}_{\pm},\bar{\bm{Q}}_{\pm},\bar{\bm{S}}^{\pm})=(Q^{\pm,1},S_{\pm,1},\bar{Q}_{\pm,1},\bar{S}^{\pm,1})\,. $$

The 4d supercharges ${\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}$ in (B.4) then translate to

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{Q}}={\bm{Q}}^{-}\,,\quad{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}={\bm{S}}_{-}\,. $$

in the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ language, which are the familiar supercharges that define the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm univ}(p,q)$ [18], also referred to as the universal superconformal index in SCFTs with enhanced supersymmetry [45]. In a similar way, as we explain below, incorporating the ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ supersymmetric surface defect defines a universal defect index for general ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ SCFTs.

The explicit relation between the Cartan generators in the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ subalgebra in (B.5) and those in the 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ algebra are,3737 37 For a ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ supersymmetric surface defect in ${\mathcal{N}}=4$ SYM (e.g. the GW surface defects), the bosonic generators of the ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ subalgebra are given by $\bar{\bm{J}}_{0}=\bar{J}_{0}-C$ and $Z=C+{J_{A}+J_{0}\over 3}$ .

$$ \displaystyle{L}_{0}=\frac{E+J_{1}}{2}\,,\quad\bar{L}_{0}=\frac{E-J_{1}}{2}\,,\quad\bar{\bm{J}}_{0}=J_{2}+\frac{3}{2}r\,,\quad Z=-J_{2}-\frac{r}{2}\,, $$

where $L_{0},\bar{L}_{0}$ are 2d conformal generators as defined before, $\bar{\bm{J}}_{0}$ is the generator for the right-moving $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ R-symmetry, $Z$ generates the $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}$ factor, and

$$ \displaystyle r={R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}\over 3} $$

is the generator for the $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{r}$ symmetry in the 4d ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal algebra. The 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ supercharges are identified with the four supercharges $({\bm{Q}}^{-},{\bm{S}}_{-},\bar{\bm{Q}}_{-},\bar{\bm{S}}^{-})$ in the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ superconformal algebra, which include (B.7) as desired. Therefore, the ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,2)$ supersymmetric surface defect defines a refinement of the ${\mathcal{N}}=1$ (universal) superconformal index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm univ}(p,q)$ with the same set of fugacities $p,q$ as long as $\mathfrak{u}(1)_{Z}$ in (B.5) is preserved.

## Appendix C Details on the 4d-2d index

### C.1 Generalities on the defect superconformal index

The 2d surface defect considered in this paper is half-BPS, which realizes a centrally extended 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ superalgebra embedded in the 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ superconformal algebra (see Appendix B). The superconformal index for the coupled system, namely the defect index (1.23) counting states in the defect Hilbert space ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathcal{D}}}(S^{3})$ , is a supersymmetric partition function on $S^{1}\times S^{3}$ with the surface defect wrapping a temporal $T^{2}$ . We will work with the GLSM description of the GW surface defect below.

The contributions from the degrees of freedom localized on the surface defect to ${\mathcal{I}}_{{\mathcal{D}}}$ can be written in term of a 2d superconformal index defined as

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\rm 2d}=\textrm{Tr}_{\text{NSNS}}\left[(-1)^{F}e^{-\beta\{{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}\}}e^{2\pi i\tau_{2d}L_{0}}e^{2\pi izJ_{0}}e^{2\pi i\chi J_{A}}e^{2\pi iuC}\right], $$

where $\tau_{2d}$ is the complex structure of the worldvolume $T^{2}$ and the trace is taken over the 2d states in the NSNS sector (i.e. satisfying anti-periodic boundary condition for both left- and right-moving modes along the equator $S^{1}\subset S^{3}$ ). The BPS condition for the 2d index $\{{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}\}=2\bar{L}_{0}-\bar{J}_{0}+C=0$ coincides with that for the 4d index (1.2) by construction.

In (C.1), the 2d bosonic charges that commute with ${\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}$ are related to the 4d charges by (B.2). Accordingly, by comparing (C.1) with (1.2), we deduce the following dictionary between the 4d and 2d chemical potentials (fugacities)

$$ \displaystyle\sigma=\tau_{2d}\,,\quad\tau=\frac{\tau_{2d}}{2}-u\,,\quad\Delta_{1}=\frac{\tau_{2d}}{2}+2\chi-u\,,\quad\Delta_{2}=\frac{\tau_{2d}}{2}+z-2\chi\,. $$

The GLSMs that engineer the GW surface defects in ${\rm SU}(N)$ SYM are ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ linear quiver gauge theories with bifundamental hypermultiplets between consecutive quiver nodes. For the surface defect that corresponds to a probe D3 brane in the bulk (which is our focus in the main text), this GLSM is simply ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED with $N$ hypermultiplets. In ${\mathcal{N}}=(2,2)$ notation, we denote the ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ hypermultiplet as $(B,\tilde{B})$ which packages two ${\mathcal{N}}=(2,2)$ chiral multiplets in conjugate representations of the gauge (flavor) symmetry, and write the ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ vector multiplet as $(\mathcal{S},{\mathcal{V}})$ where $\mathcal{S}$ is another chiral multiplet and ${\mathcal{V}}$ is a ${\mathcal{N}}=(2,2)$ vector multiplet (equivalent to a twisted chiral multiplet).

The charges of the GLSM fields under the Cartan generators of (B.1) can be fixed from the explicit coupling between the 2d GLSM and the 4d SYM fields (see e.g. [95]). ### C.2 Comparison to previous results

The defect superconformal index for a different type of surface defect preserving the same symmetry (B.1) was studied in [96] for ${\rm U}(N)$ SYM. Here the surface defect is described directly by coupling 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ hypermultiplets in the fundamental representation of ${\rm U}(N)$ to the bulk 4d ${\rm U}(N)$ SYM, we will refer to it as the free-hyper surface defect. This is physically distinct from the Gukov-Witten surface defects we study in this paper which have well-defined holographic duals as D3-branes in the type IIB string theory. Nonetheless, at the level of the 4d-2d description of the surface defect, the free-hyper surface defect only differs from the GW surface defect of the Levi-type $L=[1,N-1]$ by the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ $\rm{U}(1)$ gauge interaction on the defect worldvolume. Therefore we naively expect to obtain the same answer in the leading large $N$ limit. Below we connect the computation in [96] to our calculation here and comment on the differences and relations.

In [96], a different set of linearly independent bosonic charges was chosen to express the defect superconformal index (1.23),

$$ \mathcal{I}_{{\mathcal{D}}}=\textrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}_{{\mathcal{D}}}(S^{3})}\left[(-1)^{F}e^{-\beta\{{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}\}}t^{2(\tilde{E}+\tilde{j}_{1})}y^{2\tilde{j}_{2}}v^{\tilde{R}_{2}}w^{\tilde{R}_{3}}\right]\,. $$

These charges in [96] (which we denote with an extra tilde) are related to the ones here by,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}=E\,,\quad\tilde{j}_{1}=\frac{J_{1}+J_{2}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{j}_{2}=\frac{J_{1}-J_{2}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{R}_{1}=\frac{R_{2}+R_{1}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{R}_{2}=\frac{R_{1}-R_{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\tilde{R}_{3}=\frac{R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{C}=-J_{2}-\frac{R_{1}}{2}\,. $$

The relation between the chemical potentials in [96] and our convention follows by comparing (1.23) and (C.3),

$$ e^{2\pi i\sigma}=t^{3}y\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\tau}=\frac{t^{3}}{y}\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\Delta_{1}}=t^{2}v\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\Delta_{2}}=\frac{t^{2}w}{v}\,. $$

By explicitly enumerating the single-particle letters, the contribution to the defect index from the hypermultiplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ is obtained in the form of a Plethystic exponential, which then produces an explicit form of the modified unitary matrix model for the defect index [96].

Let us point out a few differences between the 2d index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\text{2d}}$ expression (3.14) considered in this paper for the GW surface defect and the Plethystic exponential expression for the free-hyper defect insertion in [96]. Firstly, the bosonic zero-modes of the hypermultiplet fields $b,\tilde{b}$ were manually excluded from the 2d index calculation in [96], while these fields have been taken into account in (3.14). At a technical level, including these contributions makes it possible to write the Plethystic exponential in terms of the $\theta_{0}$ -functions that produce the desired modular and elliptic properties (in particular periodicity upon certain integer shifts of the chemical potentials, see e.g. (F.1)). Furthermore we find that including these modes is crucial to reproduce the gravity answer in the holographic dual.3838 38 As mentioned in the Introduction, the GW surface defect is dual to the probe D3 brane with Neumann boundary condition for its AdS3 gauge field. On the other hand, we expect the analog of the free-hyper surface defect in the SU $(N)$ SYM to be dual to the case with Dirichlet boundary condition for the AdS3 gauge field. In particular, there is a residual U $(1)$ global symmetry and decoupled 2d degrees of freedom on this free-hyper defect, unlike the GW surface defect. We thank Ofer Aharony for discussions on this point. Secondly, the contribution from the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ vector multiplet $(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{S})$ is missing for the free-hyper defect in [96] by construction. Relatedly, unlike the GW surface defect, the ${\rm U}(1)$ subgroup of the ${\rm U}(N)$ symmetry of the free hypermultiplets is gauged not by the 2d vector multiplet but instead by the 4d vector multiplet in the bulk SYM [96], and consequently the corresponding 2d contribution ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm 2d}$ to the defect index (compared to (3.14)) has not been projected to the ${\rm U}(1)$ -singlet sector.

### C.3 2d contribution to the defect index from the elliptic genus

Here we briefly review the calculation of the elliptic genus of 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED with a pair of hypermultiplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ with charge $\pm 1$ . Upon spectral flow, this will produce the 2d contribution ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm 2d}$ to the defect index for the Gukov-Witten surface defect that corresponds to a probe D3-brane in the bulk.

The elliptic genus is an important invariant defined for general 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,1)$ supersymmetric QFTs (SQFTs) that is preserved under supersymmetry preserving deformations such as supersymmetric RG flows. It is typically defined in the RR sector of the 2d SQFT where the left- and right-moving fermions have periodic boundary conditions along the spatial ${\rm S}^{1}$ . Here, for the ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ GLSM that describes the surface defect, the fully refined elliptic genus takes the following form,

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}\equiv\text{Tr}_{\text{RR}}\,(-1)^{F}e^{2\pi i\tau_{\text{2d}}L_{0}}e^{-2\pi i\bar{\tau}_{\text{2d}}\bar{L}_{0}}e^{2\pi iz_{\text{R}}J_{0}}e^{2\pi i\chi J_{A}}e^{2\pi iuC}\,, $$

where the bosonic charges and chemical potentials are as defined in Appendix C.1.

General discussions on how to compute the elliptic genus for GLSMs can be found in [88, 125, 124]. The main point is that ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm RR}$ can be written as an integral over the holonomies of the gauge fields on the spacetime torus $T^{2}$ with complex structure $\tau_{\rm 2d}=\sigma$ where the integrand is given by a product of one-loop determinants that capture the fluctuations. This general formula was derived in [125, 124] by supersymmetric localization (see also the review [173]). Here, specializing to the case of ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED with $N$ unit-charge hypermultiplets, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}= \displaystyle\int d{\bm{u}}\,\frac{2\pi(\eta(\tau_{\text{2d}}))^{3}}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-z_{\text{R}})}\frac{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-2\chi)}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|z_{\text{R}}-2\chi)} \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-{\bm{u}}+u_{i}+\chi-z_{\text{R}}\right)\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|{\bm{u}}-u_{i}+\chi-z_{\text{R}}\right)}{\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-{\bm{u}}+u_{i}+\chi\right)\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|{\bm{u}}-u_{i}+\chi\right)}\,, $$

where $\eta(\tau_{\text{2d}})$ denotes the Dedekind eta function and $\theta_{1}(\tau_{\rm 2d}|z)$ is a Jacobi theta function. The two terms on the first line of (C.7) come from $S$ and $\mathcal{V}$ respectively in the abelian ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ vector multiplet. The terms in the second line account for the contribution from the hypermuliplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ . The integral is over the complex variable ${\bm{u}}$ which encodes the independent holonomies of the abelian gauge field on $T^{2}$ ,

$$ {\bm{u}}=\oint_{S^{1}}dx^{0}\,A_{0}-\sigma\oint_{S^{1}}dx^{1}\,A_{1}\,,\quad{\bm{u}}\in{{\mathbb{C}}/({\mathbb{Z}}+\sigma{\mathbb{Z}})}\,, $$

where the periodic identifications on $\bm{u}$ come from the large gauge transformations.

The complex holonomy integral (e.g. (C.7)) can be further reduced to a contour integral on the torus of abelian holonomies and the latter can be evaluated by the Jeffery-Kirwan residue prescription [124, 125, 173]. In the case of ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED, this amounts to collecting the residues at the $N$ simple poles in (C.7) associated to the positive-charged field at ${\bm{u}}=u_{i}-\chi$ . The final answer is

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{i\neq j}\frac{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}+z_{\text{R}}-2\chi)\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}-z_{\text{R}})}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij})\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}-2\chi)}\,, $$

where $u_{ij}\equiv u_{i}-u_{j}$ . This expression already appeared in [125] and is here written in terms of the chemical potentials in our conventions.

Instead of doing the integral over holonomy $\bm{u}$ exactly using the Jeffery-Kirwan residue prescription, we can also fix the value of $\bm{u}$ , perform the large $N$ analysis of the integrand in (C.7) and eventually integrate over $\bm{u}$ . We found that both in the empty AdS phase and the black hole phase, $\bm{u}=0$ dominates the integral. This justifies our choice in the gravity analysis of Section 2 to focus on the simplest D3-brane configuration with no worldvolume gauge field turned on.

## Appendix D Direct evaluation of the defect at the black hole saddle

In this appendix, we present a different route to derive the large $N$ limit answer (3.43) of the 2d defect expectation value at the black hole saddle. The difference from the main text is that here we don’t perform modular transformations on the following expression

$$ \mathcal{I}_{2d}=\sum_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}\,\,\prod_{(\hat{i},\hat{j})\neq(\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*})}\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}+\frac{2\sigma}{3}-\frac{\tau}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}-u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}+\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{\tau}{3}+\frac{2}{3})}{\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}+\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{2\tau}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}-u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}})}\,, $$

but rather attempt to evaluate it directly. Of course, in the end we will land on the same final answer. The goal of this appendix is to provide a sanity check, while also providing a different method that could potentially be useful for other purposes.

The red point marked inside the parallelogram corresponds to $u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}$ , which labels each individual term of the sum in (D.1). In (b), we draw a new shaded parallelogram, which represents the difference $u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}$ . Note that the red point now sits at the origin. In order to absorb the $\tilde{u}_{*}$ parameter in (D.3) into $y$ , we cut the parallelogram along the dashed red line in $\tau$ direction, the left end of which lies on the real axis. In (c), we shift the parallelogram below the dashed red line by $\sigma$ and glue two parallelograms together again. Since the expression (D.1) is invariant under $u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}\rightarrow u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}+\sigma$ , the move from (b) to (c) will not change the final result. What’s remaining is an off-set on the real axis, labelled by $u_{*}>0$ , which cannot be simply removed.*

As in Section 3.3, we parametrize the saddle point of the holonomies in the continuum limit as $u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}=x\tau+y\sigma$ . For fixed $u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}=x^{*}\tau+y^{*}\sigma\in\mathbb{C}$ , we can always rewrite $u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}=\tilde{u}_{*}\sigma+u_{*}$ , such that $\tilde{u}_{*},u_{*}\in\mathbb{R}$ . Explicitly, we have

$$ \tilde{u}_{*}=x^{*}\frac{\text{Im}(\tau)}{\text{Im}(\sigma)}+y^{*},\quad u_{*}=x^{*}\left(\tau-\sigma\frac{\text{Im}(\tau)}{\text{Im}(\sigma)}\right). $$

The difference between $u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}$ and $u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}$ in the large- $N$ limit can be expressed in terms of $x,y,\tilde{u}_{*},u_{*}$

$$ u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}=x\tau+(y-\tilde{u}_{*})\sigma-u_{*}. $$

Note that the summand in (D.1) is invariant under each individual shift $u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}\rightarrow u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}+\sigma$ . Therefore, the constant $\tilde{u}_{*}$ can always be absorbed into $y$ via this kind of shift. We demonstrate this shift explicitly in Figure 7 by cutting the parallelogram along the $\tau$ direction into two parts, shifting the lower part by $\sigma$ and gluing them back together.

On the other hand, the dependence on $u_{*}$ in (D.3) cannot be simply removed. The situation here is different from the 4D index $\mathcal{I}_{4d}$ , where the argument of (1.6) is both periodic in the $\tau$ and $\sigma$ direction. Here we only have periodicity in the $\sigma$ direction. Therefore we will carry $u_{*}$ through the calculation. Since in the index we need to sum over all possible choices of $u_{\hat{i}^{*},\hat{j}^{*}}$ , the large $N$ value of the 2d index should be given by extremizing over all possible values of $u_{*}$ . With all this in mind, the explicit expression for the defect expectation value in the large $N$ limit reads

$$ \displaystyle\frac{-\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}= \displaystyle-\underset{u_{*}}{\textrm{ext}}\int_{0}^{1}dx\int_{0}^{1}dy\,\left[\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)\tau+\left(y+\frac{2}{3}\right)\sigma-u_{*}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.+\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|\left(\frac{1}{3}-x\right)\tau+\left(\frac{1}{3}-y\right)\sigma+u_{*}+\frac{2}{3}\right)-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|-x\tau-y\sigma+u_{*}\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|\left(x-\frac{2}{3}\right)\tau+\left(y+\frac{1}{3}\right)\sigma-u_{*}-\frac{1}{3}\right)\right]. $$

One way to evaluate the integral is to rewrite the $\theta_{0}$ -functions into Plethystic exponential form, similar to what we did in the main text. As discussed in Section 3.3, we need to make sure that the Plethystic exponential expression is convergent. Similar to what we did there, we need to use the periodicity of the $\theta_{0}$ function listed in Appendix G to shift the arguments of each $\theta_{0}$ function into the convergent region. To simplify the discussion, here we again assume $\tau\in\mathbb{R}+i0^{+}$ . This assumption makes the calculation simpler but is not necessary. The final expression we derive is an analytic function of $\tau$ so it can be simply continued to general values of $\tau$ . The relevant transformations for the four $\theta_{0}$ ’s in (D.4) are performed as follows

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)\tau+\left(y+\frac{2}{3}\right)\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right.-u_{*}\right) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|(x-\frac{1}{3})\tau+(y+\frac{2}{3})\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right.-u_{*}\right),&y\in[0,\frac{1}{3}),\\
e^{-2\pi i\left[\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)\tau+\left(y-\frac{1}{3}\right)\sigma-\frac{1}{6}-u_{*}\right]}\times\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|(x-\frac{1}{3})\tau+(y-\frac{1}{3})\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right.-u_{*}\right),&y\in[\frac{1}{3},1],\end{cases} $$

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|\left(-x+\frac{1}{3}\right)\tau+\left(-y+\frac{1}{3}\right)\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right.+u_{*}\right) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|(-x+\frac{1}{3})\tau+(-y+\frac{1}{3})\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right.+u_{*}\right),&y\in[0,\frac{1}{3}),\\

$$ \theta_{0}(\sigma|-x\tau-y\sigma+u_{*})=e^{2\pi i(-x\tau-y\sigma+\frac{1}{2}+u_{*})}\theta_{0}(\sigma|-x\tau+(1-y)\sigma+u_{*}), $$

$$ \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\int_{0}^{1}dy\,\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|\left(\frac{1}{3}-x\right)\tau+\left(\frac{1}{3}-y\right)\sigma+u_{*}+\frac{2}{3}\right.\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{2\pi i(2\sigma+\tau-6u_{*}-1)}{9}-\frac{\pi i}{3\sigma\tau}\left[-B_{3}\left(\frac{\tau}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+u_{*}\right)+B_{3}\left(-\frac{2\tau}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+u_{*}\right)\right] $$

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\int_{0}^{1}dy\,\log\theta_{0}(\sigma|-x\tau-y\sigma+u_{*})=\pi i(1+2u_{*}-\sigma-\tau)-\frac{\pi i}{3\sigma\tau}\left(B_{3}(u_{*})+B_{3}(\tau-u_{*})\right) $$

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\int_{0}^{1}dy\,\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|\left(x-\frac{2}{3}\right)\tau+\left(y+\frac{1}{3}\right)\sigma-u_{*}-\frac{1}{3}\right.\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\pi i(-\sigma+\tau+6u_{*}-1)}{9}-\frac{\pi i}{3\sigma\tau}\left[-B_{3}\left(-\frac{\tau}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+u_{*}\right)+B_{3}\left(\frac{2\tau}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+u_{*}\right)\right]. $$

Adding the results of (D.13) - (D.16) together, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{-\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N} \displaystyle=\underset{u_{*}}{\textrm{ext}}\left[\frac{2\pi i(2-\sigma-2\tau)}{9}-\frac{2\pi i(\tau-1)^{2}}{9\sigma}+i\pi\frac{u_{*}^{2}}{\sigma\tau}\right]. $$

The extremum of $u_{*}$ sits at $u_{*}=0$ . Note that since $\textrm{Re}\left(i/(\sigma\tau)\right)\propto\textrm{Im}\left(\sigma\tau\right)>0$ , $u_{*}=0$ minimizes the real part of the action and therefore gives the dominant contribution. Setting $u_{*}=0$ , we recover the final answer

$$ \frac{-\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}=-\frac{2\pi i(\sigma+\tau-1)^{2}}{9\sigma}. $$

This agrees with our final answer (3.43) in the main text.

## Appendix E Field theory analysis in the $\sigma=\tau$ limit

In the main part of this paper, we focused on the range of chemical potentials (3.17), where the 2d index formula (3.16) has a convergent Plethystic exponential expression, assuming that the ${\rm SU}(N)$ holonomies take real values. Within this range, we find agreement between the bulk and boundary analysis.

However, the range of chemical potential (3.17) excludes the special limit $\sigma=\tau,\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{3}=(2\sigma-1)/3$ . If we naively apply the index formula (3.16) outside the range (3.17) and in particular to the $\sigma=\tau$ limit, we encounter subtleties that we are not sure how to resolve. Intriguingly, instead of the more intricate analysis for the black hole saddle, it is for the thermal AdS saddle that we appear to find an surprising answer. In this appendix we present the puzzling computation and discuss some possible interpretations. We leave a satisfying resolution to future study.

For convenience, here we write down the expression for the 2d index that we will evaluate (after specifying to the case $\sigma=\tau$ ):

$$ \mathcal{I}_{2d}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij}+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{2}{3})}{\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij})}. $$

### E.1 Thermal AdS saddle

As explained in section 3, the thermal AdS saddle corresponds to the eigenvalue distribution $u_{j}=\frac{j}{N},j=0,...,N-1$ . For the purpose of evaluating the large $N$ limit of $\mathcal{I}_{2d}$ , we’d like to write the $\theta_{0}$ functions into Plethystic exponential form. Since all $u_{i}$ are real, in order to make $\theta_{0}$ -functions have convergent Plethystic exponentials, we need to shift the argument of $\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3})$ using identity (G.5)

$$ \theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\right.-\frac{1}{3}\right)=-e^{2\pi i\left(u_{ji}-\frac{1}{3}\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)}\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|u_{ji}+\frac{2\sigma}{3}\right.-\frac{1}{3}\right). $$

After this shift on the argument, all $\theta_{0}$ -functions appear in (E.1) have valid Plethystic exponentials. Based on the same argument made in section 3.2, Plethystic exponentials evaluated at the thermal AdS saddle always contribute $e^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ factors to the 2d index. Therefore, the large- $N$ contributions purely come from the prefactor in (E.2). In this case, we find that

$$ -\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=-2\pi iN\left(\frac{1}{3}\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)+\mathcal{O}(1), $$

which has a nonvanishing $O(N)$ term. It seems to suggest a nonzero brane action, despite being on the thermal AdS background. We are not aware of a possible interpretation of this nonzero action.

One possible resolution to this is that one should first evaluate the large $N$ limit of the field theory expression within the range (3.17), then analytically continue the large $N$ action to the $\sigma=\tau$ limit. This would lead to an answer that is simply zero which agrees with what we would expect from gravity. However, it is unclear to us what the physical motivation of such a prescription is. Of course, another possibility is that (E.3) does have a gravity interpretation.

### E.2 Black hole saddle

When $\sigma=\tau$ , the supersymmetric black hole solution is associated to the $(1,0)$ saddle of the matrix integral[33], which can also be derived from the roots of the Bethe-ansatz equation[58, 25]. The eigenvalue $u_{j}$ is distributed uniformly on the line in $\sigma$ direction, i.e. $u_{j}=\frac{j}{N}\sigma,j=0,...,N-1$ . This distribution of $u_{j}$ is different from directly the distribution obtained by taking the collinear limit $\sigma\rightarrow\tau$ of the parallelogram ansatz used in Section 3. In [48], the relation between the solutions of two ansatz was studied, and it was shown that the large- $N$ contribution from both approaches agree. In this part of discussion, we use the saddle-point distribution from BAEs for simplicity, and in the end we will see that the result is consistent with the collinear limit of the analytic continuation of the result in Section 3. Note that the expression (E.1) is invariant under $u_{i}\rightarrow u_{i}+\sigma$ shift, all terms in the summation over $i$ should be identical. In the large- $N$ limit, we rewrite the 2d index into the following integral expression

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx\left[-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|x\sigma+\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right.\right)-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|-x\sigma+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\right.\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.+\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|x\sigma-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\right.\right)+\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|-x\sigma\right.\right)\right]. $$

In order to evaluate this integral, we could adopt the same procedure as we use in Appendix D to write the $\theta_{0}$ -functions into convergent Plethystic exponentials by shifting the arguments suitably. After performing the shifts, we decompose the integral into the following parts

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}= \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dx\log\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma\right)} \displaystyle+2\pi i\int_{\frac{2}{3}}^{1}dx\,\left(x\sigma-\frac{2\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{6}\right)-2\pi i\int_{\frac{2}{3}}^{1}dx\,\left(-x\sigma+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\right) \displaystyle+2\pi i\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{3}}dx\,\left(x\sigma-\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\right)+2\pi i\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\left(-x\sigma+\frac{1}{2}\right). $$

The first line admits the convergent Plethystic exponential expression, so we can integrate out $x$ and write the result in terms of dilogarithm functions

$$ \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dx\log\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma\right)}= \displaystyle\frac{i}{2\pi\sigma}\left[\text{Li}_{2}(e^{\frac{4\pi i}{3}})+\text{Li}_{2}(e^{-\frac{4\pi i}{3}})-2\text{Li}_{2}(1)\right], $$

where we use the series expansion of dilogarithm $\text{Li}_{2}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^{n}}{n^{2}}$ . For dilogarithm function, we have the following useful identity

$$ \textrm{Li}_{2}(e^{2\pi iz})+\textrm{Li}_{2}(e^{-2\pi iz})=2\pi^{2}B_{2}(z),\quad 0\leq\textrm{Re}(z)<1, $$

where $B_{2}(z)$ is the second Bernoulli polynomial. By applying this identity to the dilogarithms in the $-\log\mathcal{I}_{\text{2d}}$ expression, we obtain the following leading term in the large- $N$ expansion

$$ -\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}=-\frac{2\pi i}{9\sigma}-\frac{8\pi i}{9}(\sigma-1)=-\frac{2\pi i(2\sigma-1)^{2}}{9\sigma}, $$

which agrees with the result derived in (3.43) provided that $\sigma$ is equal to $\tau$ . Therefore, in this case, the final expression (E.8) is still consistent with the D3-brane effective action (2.37) evaluated in the black hole background.

## Appendix F Defects on shifted chemical potential saddle points

As we have mentioned in the main text, an important conceptual point in the recent discussion of the ${1\over 16}$ -BPS index and its gravity dual is the importance of saddle points with shifted chemical potentials. These are gravity solutions with the same fugacities but different chemical potentials at infinity, and the sum over them is important in reproducing the expected periodicity of the field theory index. This is very clear if we wrote the field theory expression in terms of a trace. After transforming to a microcanonical ensemble in the charges, this periodicity property implies the correct discreteness of the charge spectrum (in the original superconformal index or in the case with a surface operator insertion). The existence of these extra saddles is thus a field theory motivated constraint on the “sum over geometries” as expected of a gravitational path integral. In cases such as the near extremal or near BPS limits of the gravity path integral, the sum over these shifted saddles is not suppressed, and they have important consequences for the low energy physics [74, 49, 127, 75].

Given the chemical potentials $\sigma,\tau,\Delta_{a},a=1,2,3$ on the field theory side, one can generally consider infinitely many gravity solutions with chemical potentials $\sigma_{g},\,\tau_{g},\,\Delta_{a,g},\,a=1,2,3$ shifted relative to the field theory ones by independent integers (while satisfying the constraint $\sigma_{g}+\tau_{g}-\Delta_{1,g}-\Delta_{2,g}-\Delta_{3,g}=\pm 1$ ). Here we used subscript $g$ to highlight that the chemical potentials showing up in gravity can be distinct from the ones at the boundary. Even though these gravity solutions formally exist, their stability and the convergence of the sum over them are generally unclear. More essential to our consideration here, the full characterization of these solutions on the field theory side, in particular, in the language of large $N$ saddle points for the unitary matrix integral [48] (see e.g. [45] for a different approach using Thermal Bethe Ansatz), is still under active research and have not been fully understood to our best knowledge.

It is natural to wonder about how the defect/D3-brane behaves on these other saddles. We will restrict our attention to the case where

$$ \sigma_{g}=\sigma+3n_{1},\quad\tau_{g}=\tau+3n_{2},\quad\Delta_{1,g}=\Delta_{2,g}=\Delta_{3,g}=\frac{\sigma+\tau-1}{3}+n_{1}+n_{2},\quad n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}, $$

so that the black hole solution still has the same R-charges and can be described by the same metric as in Section 2.4040 40 Notice that not all of these gravity solutions are stable. For the case with $\sigma=\tau$ , it was shown in [45] that the action can be lower by adding wrapped Euclidean D3 branes unless $\sigma_{g}=\tau_{g}$ . We thank Ofer Aharony and Ohad Mamroud for comments on this point. The only difference is that the chemical potentials in Section 2 are now replaced by the ones with subscript $g$ and the rest of the analysis goes through. Therefore, following (2.37), the action of the D3-brane on the shifted gravity saddles, after regularization, is

$$ I_{D3,\textrm{E, finite}}=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma_{g}+\tau_{g}-1)^{2}}{9\sigma_{g}}=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma+\tau+3(n_{1}+n_{2})-1)^{2}}{9(\sigma+3n_{1})}. $$

On the field theory side, [48] proposed a family of large $N$ saddle points that naturally correspond to (F.1). These saddle points are characterized by a uniform parallelogram distribution of holonomies $u_{i}$ , similar to what we considered in (3.3), but with two edges of the parallelogram given by $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2}$ . It was claimed in [48] that this new parallelogram saddle would satisfy the large $N$ saddle point equations of the unitary matrix model, with the shifted chemical potentials, namely $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2},\Delta_{a}+n_{1}+n_{2},a=1,2,3$ satisfying the same inequalities that the chemical potentials should satisfy for the original saddle point.4141 41 See (2.41) of [48] for the detailed form of the inequalitites. We thank Seok Kim for correspondence on these points. Therefore, we have

$$ \langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{2(\sigma+3n_{1})}{3}-\frac{\tau+3n_{2}}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ij}+\frac{\sigma+3n_{1}}{3}+\frac{\tau+3n_{2}}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{\sigma+3n_{1}}{3}-\frac{2(\tau+3n_{2})}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij})}, $$

where $u_{i}=u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}=\frac{\hat{i}}{\sqrt{N}}(\sigma+3n_{1})+\frac{\hat{j}}{\sqrt{N}}(\tau+3n_{2})$ . One might be puzzled by the explicit shift of the chemical potentials in (F.3), but since we have $\theta_{0}(\sigma|x+1)=\theta_{0}(\sigma|x)$ , the shifts in (F.3) should not affect the final answer, given that $n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}$ . This is of course true, but the benefit of (F.3) is to highlight that the shifted chemical potentials $\sigma+3n_{1},...$ should be within the same range as the chemical potentials for which the discussion in Section 3.3 would be valid. The calculation then follows exactly the discussion in Section 3.3, with the chemical potentials replaced by the shifted ones. From (3.43), this yields a final answer

$$ -\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma+\tau+3(n_{1}+n_{2})-1)^{2}}{9(\sigma+3n_{1})}, $$

which agrees with (F.2).

However, we want to highlight an unsatisfying feature of this discussion. Generally, after we fix the values of $\sigma,\tau,\Delta_{a}$ which lie within the inequalities in [48], the shifted chemical potentials $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2},\Delta_{a}+n_{1}+n_{2}$ will not satisfy the same inequalities and therefore we cannot apply the parallelogram ansatz. To make it more clear, in the above field theory calculation, we are not considering the shifted saddles for the same chemical potentials, but rather shifted saddles for correspondingly different chemical potentials. This appears to be different from the gravity picture where we can consider both the original saddle and the shifted ones for a fixed set of chemical potential. Therefore, the results in this appendix shouldn’t be taken as a match between field theory side and the gravity side, but rather as only preliminary evidence. Nonetheless, we would like to emphasize that the difficulty of relating the two is already present at the level of the original BPS index, and not particularly related to the added defect. It would also be useful to understand whether one can apply different techniques, such as the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz [45] to compute the 4d-2d index.

## Appendix G Conventions and relations for $\theta$ -functions

The Plethystic exponential, which usually appears in the index calculation, is defined as follows:

$$ \textrm{PE}\left(\frac{a}{1-q}\right)\equiv\exp\left[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}\frac{a^{n}}{1-q^{n}}\right]. $$

Provided the above definition, we can associate the Plethystic exponential to the $q$ -Pochhammer symbol

$$ (a;q)_{\infty}\equiv\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-aq^{k})=\frac{1}{\textrm{PE}\left(\frac{a}{1-q}\right)} $$

We introduce one useful special function $\theta_{0}$ in terms of the product of two $q$ -Pochhammer symbols

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=\left(e^{2\pi iu};e^{2\pi i\tau}\right)_{\infty}\left(e^{2\pi i(\tau-u)};e^{2\pi i\tau}\right)_{\infty} $$

By massaging the two Plethystic exponentials in (G.3) together, we obtain a series expansion for $\log{\theta_{0}}$

$$ \log\theta_{0}(\tau|u)=-i\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\cos{n\pi(2u-\tau)}}{n\sin{n\pi\tau}}. $$

Note that the above Plethystic exponential expression does not always have a convergent exponent. The formula (G.1) is only valid when $|q|,|a|<1$ . Therefore, the $\theta_{0}$ -function can be rewritten as a Plethystic exponential only if $\text{Im}(\tau)>0,\,0<\text{Im}(u)<\text{Im}(\tau)$ . The same criterion also works for the series expansion of $\log{\theta_{0}}$ .

The $\theta_{0}$ -function has the following quasi-periodicity property:

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=\theta_{0}(\tau|u+1)=-e^{2\pi iu}\theta_{0}(\tau|u+\tau). $$

Moreover, the $\theta_{0}$ -function possesses a few modular properties under the transformations $\tau\rightarrow\tau+1$ ( $T$ ) and $u\rightarrow\frac{u}{\tau},\,\tau\rightarrow-\frac{1}{\tau}$ ( $S$ )

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau|u)= \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau+1|u), \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau|u)= \displaystyle e^{\pi iB_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)}\theta_{0}\left(-\frac{1}{\tau}\left|\frac{u}{\tau}\right.\right), $$

where $B_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)$ is the multiple Bernoulli polynomial defined as follows:

$$ B_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)=-\frac{B_{2}(u+1)}{\tau}+B_{1}(u+1)-\frac{\tau}{6}. $$

The $B_{1}(x)=x-\frac{1}{2}$ and $B_{2}(x)=x^{2}-x+\frac{1}{6}$ are ordinary Bernoulli polynomials.

Besides the $\theta_{0}$ -function, we introduce the ordinary Jacobi Theta function $\theta_{1}$ , which can be obtained from the $\theta_{0}$ -function via the following identity:

$$ \theta_{1}(\tau|u)=ie^{-i\pi(u-\tau/4)}(q;q)\theta_{0}(\tau|u). $$

The Jacobi theta function $\theta_{1}$ has the following double quasi-periodicity:

$$ \theta_{1}(\tau|u+a+b\tau)=(-1)^{a+b}e^{-2\pi ibu-i\pi b^{2}\tau}\theta_{1}(\tau|u). $$

Here we summarize the zeroes and poles of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ , which is useful in performing the contour integral over the worldvolume gauge field. $\theta_{0}(\sigma|u)$ has no poles, while it has zeroes at $u=a+b\tau$ . The derivative of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ near $u=0$ is

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)^{\prime}|_{u=0}=-2\pi i(q;q)^{2}. $$

According to the residue theorem, we have the following contour integral

$$ \oint_{u=0}\frac{du}{\theta_{0}(\tau|u)}=-\frac{1}{(q;q)^{2}}. $$

Another important identity of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ is

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=-e^{2\pi iu}\theta_{0}(\tau|-u). $$

This property can be derived directly from the definition of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ in (G.3).
